documents.title: Sample Generative AI Syllabus Statements
tiers: Level 2 AI-assisted idea generation and structuring
Level 4 AI task completion, human evaluation
documents.summary: The UMSL Center for Teaching and Learning offers instructors sample generative AI syllabus statements, from UMSL courses and from UMass Amherst, Temple and Washington University. They span a five-level AI Assessment Scale, limited-use and prohibit statements, and advice on penalties and conversations with students. The content of each policy is left to the instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'The content of your policy is up to you' and offers sample statements ranging from prohibition to full use plus a five-level AI Assessment Scale, so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors; it is tiered, hence delegates with tiers listed.

units.why: The center tells instructors that 'The content of your policy is up to you', so the AI rule is set by each instructor rather than the university; this is a delegation rule, hence P04 and not a course-level default.
units.anchor: The content of your policy is up to you
units.policy: Instructors decide the content of their own course AI policy.

units.why: The same sentence says 'transparent, curious conversations with your students about AI use ... are highly encouraged', which asks instructors to discuss the rules with students; P66 fits better than P09 because it goes beyond writing the rule in the syllabus.
units.anchor: transparent, curious conversations with your students about AI use
units.policy: Instructors are highly encouraged to hold transparent, curious conversations with students about AI use that acknowledge benefits, drawbacks, ethical concerns, and responsible use.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on actor, phase, modality and type; they differ only on unit_stance (A neutral, B encourage). The sentence encourages talking with students about AI, not AI use itself, so unit_stance is neutral.

units.why: The center 'highly recommend[s]' departmental conversations on 'appropriate penalties' including for first-time versus repeat offenders, a recommendation about setting penalties; P37 is nearest but the unit recommends discussing penalties rather than stating one.
units.anchor: have conversations in your department about the appropriate penalties
units.policy: Instructors are highly recommended to have conversations in their department about appropriate penalties for unauthorized use of AI within the scope of their course and grading.
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on all codes. B's normalized policy also covered the next sentence (first-time versus repeat offenders), which coder A coded as its own unit; the policy here is rewritten to the first sentence only ('We highly recommend that you have conversations in your department about the appropriate penalties...'), and the graduated-penalty sentence is kept as a separate unit.
units.fit_note: Recommends departments discuss penalties; no penalty is stated. | States no penalty; recommends departments deliberate over penalties and distinguish first-time from repeat offenders.

units.why: Asking instructors to think about the penalty for "first-time offenders and those who repeatedly violate" is guidance on escalation by offense, which P37 lists; no actual penalty is set.
units.anchor: appropriate level of penalty for first-time offenders and those who repeatedly violate your policies
units.fit_note: Advises thinking about graduated penalties; none are stated.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. The second sentence of the paragraph asks instructors to consider 'the appropriate level of penalty for first-time offenders and those who repeatedly violate your policies'; B merged it with the department-conversation unit. It is a separate sentence and a separate point (graduated penalties), so it is kept as its own unit, and the repeat-offender wording is removed from the first unit's policy to avoid duplication.

units.why: Sample statement: "We will use generative AI tools at various points throughout this course", so AI is built into the course. P79 fits better than P02 because use is planned in, not just allowed.
units.anchor: We will use generative AI tools at various points throughout this course
units.resolution_why: A coded actor student, B all; unit_stance A require, B encourage. The sample says 'We will use generative AI tools', a class-wide 'we' covering instructor and students, so actor is all. Use is planned into the course, which the codebook calls require.

units.why: "not to replace your own work": AI is part of skill building but must not substitute the student's own thinking, matching P32.
units.anchor: Our goal is to use AI as part of your overall skill building, not to
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. 'Our goal is...' states a principle rather than a rule applied while working, so phase is general; it neither bans nor permits a specific use, so unit_stance is neutral.

units.why: The sample says 'each assignment will include clear instructions about appropriate ways to use AI', i.e. a statement of AI expectations in assignment instructions; this is P09.
units.anchor: each assignment will include clear instructions about appropriate ways to use AI
units.resolution_why: Found only by B (A put this sentence and the scale in one unit). The sentence says 'each assignment will include clear instructions about appropriate ways to use AI', a commitment to state AI expectations in assignment instructions, separate from the scale that explains them. Kept as P09; the scale stays a separate P05 unit.

units.why: The sample ties each assignment to 'the AI Assessment Scale', a named five-level scale; naming tiers is P05 rather than P09 because the point is the scale of levels.
units.anchor: explained with the AI Assessment Scale included below
units.policy: Appropriate AI use on each assignment is explained with the AI Assessment Scale (levels 1 to 5).
units.resolution_why: A coded one unit for the whole sentence ('each assignment will include clear instructions ... explained with the AI Assessment Scale') as P05; B split it into P09 (instructions) and P05 (the scale). Both agree on the scale unit's codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B neutral). Naming levels is a way of organizing rules and takes no position itself, so neutral. The instructions commitment is a separate unit.

units.why: Students must "follow the AI scale" set for each assignment, i.e. learn and follow the applicable AI rules (P78).
units.anchor: require you to follow the AI scale
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. The source says 'Successful completion of the assignments will require you to follow the AI scale', a duty on students to follow the per-assignment AI level, which is real and separate from 'never replace your own work'. Kept as P78.

units.why: The sample requires students to 'never replace your own work with AI-generated responses', banning AI-produced submissions; P19 fits.
units.anchor: never replace your own work with AI-generated responses

units.why: "I will often ask you to describe or reflect on your work process, including your use of AI": a reflection on AI use is required, P26.
units.anchor: describe or reflect on your work process, including your use of AI

units.why: 'I am happy to meet with you to discuss it ... you may submit a grade appeal' gives a student flagged for integrity violations a way to contest the finding; P64 fits. The sentence recurs verbatim in two other samples and is coded once.
units.anchor: If your assignment has been flagged as violating academic integrity policy and you want to
units.policy: Students whose assignment is flagged as violating academic integrity policy can contest the assessment in a meeting with the instructor and, if unresolved, submit a grade appeal to the university.

units.why: Level 1 of the scale says 'AI must not be used at any point during the assessment', a ban on AI for that assessment; P01 fits (default ban on graded work) and nothing else is closer.
units.anchor: AI must not be used at any point during the assessment
units.fit_note: Level 1 of the named AI Assessment Scale (coded separately as P05); also a plain ban on AI for the assessment.
units.resolution_why: A coded P05 (scale level) and phase during-assessment; B coded P01 and during-work. The scale itself is coded in its own P05 unit. This sentence says 'AI must not be used at any point during the assessment', a ban on AI for the work, which P01 covers. 'Assessment' here means the graded task or assignment (the whole scale governs assignments), not an exam, so the phase is during-work.

units.why: Level 2 allows AI 'for brainstorming, creating structures, and generating ideas', a permission to explore approaches; P15 fits, while the next sentence's ban on AI content is a separate unit.
units.anchor: AI can be used in the assessment for brainstorming, creating structures, and generating ideas
units.fit_note: Tier 2 of the scale; ideation and structuring only.

units.why: Level 2 also states 'No AI content is allowed in the final submission', which bars AI-produced material in what is handed in; P19 fits.
units.anchor: No AI content is allowed in the final submission

units.why: Level 3 lets AI 'make improvements to the clarity or quality of student-created work' but 'no new content', which is editing support; P91 is the permission itself, not P18.
units.anchor: AI can be used to make improvements to the clarity or quality of student-created work
units.fit_note: Editing is allowed only if no new content is created by AI ("no new content can be created using AI").

units.why: Level 3 requires that 'your original work with no AI content must be provided in an appendix', so the student must submit their pre-AI draft; P26 (submit drafts) fits better than P24 because it is a draft, not a disclosure statement.
units.anchor: your original work with no AI content must be provided in an appendix
units.fit_note: Requires the pre-AI original work in an appendix, not a transcript or reflection.

units.why: Level 4 has AI 'complete certain elements of the task' with students giving 'discussion and commentary' and 'evaluating its output'; this permits AI-generated content under conditions (P16), with the evaluation duty noted instead of a separate P31 unit.
units.anchor: AI is used to complete certain elements of the task, with students providing discussion and
units.fit_note: Content generally, not only code; allowed only with student commentary and critical evaluation of the output (also coded as P31).

units.why: Level 4 "requires critical engagement with AI-generated content and evaluating its output", which is a duty to evaluate AI output, P31.
units.anchor: requires critical engagement with AI-generated content and evaluating its output
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. Level 4 'requires critical engagement with AI-generated content and evaluating its output': a duty to evaluate AI output, which B only noted in a fit note. It is a distinct rule, so kept as P31; unit_stance permit because it conditions the AI use Level 4 allows.

units.why: Level 4: "Any AI generated content must be cited", a disclosure duty, P24.
units.anchor: Any AI generated content must be cited.
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B require). The citation duty is a condition on AI use that Level 4 permits, so unit_stance is permit.

units.why: Level 5 "FULL AI": "You may use AI throughout your assessment", with AI as a "co-pilot": open permission and encouragement, P02.
units.anchor: You may use AI throughout your assessment to support your own work

units.why: Level 5 removes any disclosure duty ("do not have to specify which content is AI generated"). P24 is the nearest home, with a fit note that disclosure is NOT required here.
units.anchor: do not have to specify which content is AI generated
units.fit_note: States that disclosure is NOT required at this tier (Level 5).
units.resolution_why: A coded P24 with modality may; B coded P28 with modality informs. The sentence says students 'do not have to specify which content is AI generated': it is a rule about whether disclosure is required, which belongs with the disclosure-duty type P24 (as an exemption, hence the fit note). P28 is about the effect of disclosure or its absence on integrity or grading, which the sentence does not state. It grants students a freedom, so modality is may.

units.why: The limited-use sample says AI is 'permitted/encouraged as specified in assignment instructions, with proper attribution, but other uses are prohibited', so the assignment decides and everything else is banned; P04 is nearest, with the default ban and attribution in the fit note.
units.anchor: permitted/encouraged as specified in assignment instructions, with proper attribution, but other uses are prohibited
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start and modality must; B coded during-work and may. The sentence says AI 'is permitted/encouraged as specified in assignment instructions' and other uses are prohibited. The permission is the main clause and states what students may do while doing assignment work, so phase is during-work and modality may; the default ban on other uses is recorded in the fit note.
units.fit_note: Assignment-level permission combined with a ban on all other uses (P01/P06). | Also sets a default ban on uses not specified and requires attribution.

units.why: "two assignments that encourage you to practice using AI in conversation with your own critical thinking": AI is built into two assignments, P79.
units.anchor: two assignments that encourage you to practice using AI in conversation with your own critical

units.why: 'you should not use AI to brainstorm, write, or edit the work you submit' outside the listed assignments is a default restriction; P01 fits, and modality is should-not as the text says 'should not'.
units.anchor: you should not use AI to brainstorm, write, or edit the work you submit for
units.fit_note: Bans brainstorming, writing and editing with AI outside the named assignments, wider than generation alone (P19).
units.resolution_why: A coded P19 and B coded P01. Outside the two named assignments 'you should not use AI to brainstorm, write, or edit the work you submit': this is a default ban on AI for the course's work with named exceptions, which is what P01 covers. P19 is about AI producing the submitted work and does not fit as well because brainstorming and editing are also banned. Modality stays should-not as the text says 'should not'.

units.why: "This includes using AI writing/editing tools such as Grammarly" extends the ban to named prose tools, so P18 (prose rules) fits.
units.anchor: This includes using AI writing/editing tools such as Grammarly.

units.why: "You will regularly do tech-free in-class writing" is an unassisted in-class assessment component, P33; the instructor will also learn the student's voice.
units.anchor: You will regularly do tech-free in-class writing, and I will learn your writing voice.
units.resolution_why: A coded modality informs, B coded must. 'You will regularly do tech-free in-class writing' tells students what they are required to do in this course (unassisted in-class writing), so it is a requirement: must.

units.why: "do your own writing ... as part of your contract of honesty with me" asks students to submit their own work, P29.
units.anchor: to do your own writing, regardless of the assignment, as part of your contract of
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. The sentence is about the writing students submit for each assignment ('do your own writing, regardless of the assignment'), so during-work; P29 not P95 because it concerns owning submitted work.

units.why: A violating assignment 'will automatically receive no credit or feedback', a stated penalty; P37 fits, with false quotations and nonexistent citations named as further triggers.
units.anchor: it will automatically receive no credit or feedback
units.policy: An assignment that uses AI in ways that violate this policy, or has academic integrity issues such as false quotations, quotations attributed falsely or without attribution, or citations of nonexistent sources, automatically receives no credit or feedback.
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; B's normalized policy is kept, and its wording is checked against the source ('it will automatically receive no credit or feedback'). Coder A's separate false-quotations unit sits in the same sentence and is folded in here; unit_stance restrict because a stated penalty limits AI use.
units.fit_note: Also covers false quotations and citations of nonexistent sources as integrity issues (coder A coded these as a separate P31 unit with the note: framed as an integrity violation that triggers a penalty, not a duty to verify).

units.why: "We will not use AI tools for any work in this course" is a blanket ban, P01.
units.anchor: We will not use AI tools for any work in this course.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work. 'We will not use AI tools for any work in this course' is a ban that applies while doing course work, not an act of communicating expectations, so phase is during-work.

units.why: Reason one: the course "is designed to help you build the skills to think, research, write, and problem-solve independently", skill building through one's own practice, P41.
units.anchor: this course is designed to help you build the skills to think, research, write, and
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B general. The passage gives the reason for the AI ban, a principle behind the rule, so phase is general.

units.why: "Preliminary research has shown that AI use has led to cognitive debt" cites evidence about AI and learning, P55.
units.anchor: Preliminary research has shown that AI use has led to cognitive debt in academic assignments.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B general. The passage cites evidence as a rationale (informs), so phase is general.

units.why: Reason two lists "environmental costs, racial bias, and privacy concerns" as ethical risks of AI, P53.
units.anchor: AI tools pose many ethical risks, including environmental costs, racial bias, and privacy concerns
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B general. The passage states ethical risks as a rationale, so phase is general.

units.why: 'This includes the use of tools like Grammarly' applies the full ban to writing tools; P18 fits because it names a prose tool inside a prohibition.
units.anchor: This includes the use of tools like Grammarly.

units.why: 'We’ll talk about this approach in class and discuss strategies ... that do not rely on AI tools' means the instructor discusses and explains the rule; P66.
units.anchor: We’ll talk about this approach in class

units.why: 'UMSL does not currently approve any AI-detection software' says detection software is not used or approved; P39 is nearest but the unit states non-approval, not unreliability.
units.anchor: UMSL does not currently approve any AI-detection software.
units.fit_note: Says detectors are not approved; does not say they are unreliable. | Reason is non-approval by the university, not unreliability.

units.why: 'I like to operate on a trust system with students and assume the best' presumes good faith; P68 lists that as a feature.
units.anchor: I like to operate on a trust system with students and assume the best.

units.why: 'I may ask you to have an office hours meeting with me to discuss the matter' means talking with the student before sanctions; P57.
units.anchor: I may ask you to have an office hours meeting with me to discuss the

units.why: 'you may receive a failing grade on the assignment' states a penalty for apparently AI-generated work; P37.
units.anchor: you may receive a failing grade on the assignment
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence states a penalty for apparently AI-generated work, so it restricts AI use: restrict.

units.why: UMass: "all work produced for a grade will be the sole product of a student's endeavors", own-work responsibility, P29.
units.anchor: all work produced for a grade will be the sole product of a student’s endeavors
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. 'all work produced for a grade will be the sole product of a student's endeavors' applies to the work students produce for grades, so during-work.

units.why: 'Students are encouraged to use artificial intelligence among many other (re)search resources' welcomes AI as a research tool; P02.
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use artificial intelligence among many other (re)search resources

units.why: "Students must not substitute the substance of their work with the results of such (re)search tools": AI may not produce the submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: Students must not substitute the substance of their work with the results of such (re)search
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A restrict, B prohibit). The same passage encourages AI as a search resource and bars only substituting it for the substance of one's work, so the unit restricts rather than prohibits AI.

units.why: Substitution "would contravene the rules academic integrity", classing it as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: that act would contravene the rules academic integrity
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. 'that act would contravene the rules academic integrity' classes substituting AI output for one's work as an integrity breach; real and distinct from the ban unit, so kept as P36 with unit_stance restrict.

units.why: 'Course assignments are intentionally designed to stimulate and develop critical thinking and individual skills' explains why assignments call for students' own work; P41.
units.anchor: Course assignments are intentionally designed to stimulate and develop critical thinking and individual skills
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B general. The passage explains why assignments are designed as they are, a rationale, so general.

units.why: 'learners can choose to use AI tools like ChatGPT to help brainstorm and/or draft assignments ... or to revise' permits several uses; P15 is nearest, with drafting and revising in the fit note.
units.anchor: learners can choose to use AI tools like ChatGPT to help brainstorm and/or draft assignments
units.fit_note: Also permits drafting and revising existing written work (prose), not only brainstorming; limited to what assignment instructions allow. Coder A placed it at P16, which is about code and so fits less well.
units.resolution_why: A coded P16 and B coded P15. P16 is about AI-generated code; this is prose and the first named use is brainstorming ('help brainstorm and/or draft assignments or projects, or to revise existing written work'), so P15 is the nearest, with the drafting and revising in the fit note.

units.why: UMass: submissions "will follow the specific assignment instructions regarding the use of AI", students follow each assignment's rules, P78.
units.anchor: submitted assignments will follow the specific assignment instructions regarding the use of AI
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B neutral). The duty to follow each assignment's AI instructions sits in a statement that encourages AI in specific assignments, so it conditions permitted use: permit.

units.why: UMass: students "appropriately reference, cite, and attribute any role played, or text generated by AI tools", P24.
units.anchor: appropriately reference, cite, and attribute any role played, or text generated by AI tools
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B require). The citation duty conditions the AI use that the statement encourages, so permit.

units.why: The Temple sample lists 'Brainstorming and refining your ideas' among permitted uses of generative AI; P15 is the type that matches this use.
units.anchor: Brainstorming and refining your ideas

units.why: The Temple sample lists 'Finding information on your topic' among permitted uses of generative AI; P12 is the type that matches this use.
units.anchor: Finding information on your topic

units.why: The Temple sample lists 'Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts; and' among permitted uses of generative AI; P91 is the type that matches this use.
units.anchor: Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts; and

units.why: The Temple sample lists 'Checking grammar and style' among permitted uses of generative AI; P91 is the type that matches this use.
units.anchor: Checking grammar and style

units.why: The Temple sample forbids using AI for 'Impersonating you in classroom contexts', such as discussion board posts or Zoom chat; P58 covers course communication written by the student.
units.anchor: Impersonating you in classroom contexts

units.why: 'Completing group work that your group has assigned to you, unless it is mutually agreed' bars AI from doing a student's assigned part; P19 fits with the group-agreement exception in the note.
units.anchor: Completing group work that your group has assigned to you
units.fit_note: Exception when the group mutually agrees the tool may be used. Coder A judged no type covered a group-work rule (UNCOVERED: students may not use AI to do their assigned part of group work unless the group agrees); P19 is used because the AI would be doing a student's assigned work.
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED (no type for group work); B coded P19. The rule bars AI from 'Completing group work that your group has assigned to you' unless the group agrees. That is AI doing the student's assigned work for submission, which P19 states; the group-agreement exception is recorded in the fit note and A's uncovered note is kept there.

units.why: 'Writing a draft of a writing assignment' is listed as not permitted, so AI may not produce the draft; P19.
units.anchor: Writing a draft of a writing assignment.

units.why: 'Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments' is not permitted; P19.
units.anchor: Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments.

units.why: 'You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query' covers IP and misinformation; P29 fits, with the IP and misinformation duties in the note.
units.anchor: You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query
units.fit_note: Responsibility explicitly includes not violating intellectual property laws and not submitting misinformation or unethical content (also coded separately as P52).

units.why: The parenthetical names intellectual property violations, misinformation and unethical content as risks in AI output. P52 fits for IP; the fit note records the extra concerns.
units.anchor: that it does not violate intellectual property laws, or contain misinformation or unethical content
units.fit_note: Also covers misinformation and unethical content (P31, P53).
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. The parenthetical says submitted AI-based content must not 'violate intellectual property laws, or contain misinformation or unethical content'. B folded it into the P29 fit note. It is a distinct duty, so kept as P52, with the misinformation part in its fit note.

units.why: "Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited in order to stay within university policies on academic honesty", P24.
units.anchor: Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B require). The documentation duty conditions permitted AI use, so permit.

units.why: "[insert the penalty here*]" in the template: instructors are to state a penalty for unauthorized AI use, P37, with a fit note that none is stated.
units.anchor: Any assignment that is found to have used generative AI tools in unauthorized ways
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence is a template slot with the penalty left blank, so it states no position: neutral.
units.fit_note: A placeholder; no penalty is specified. | The penalty itself is a placeholder for the instructor to fill in.

units.why: 'When in doubt about permitted usage, please ask for clarification' tells students to ask when unsure; P10.
units.anchor: When in doubt about permitted usage, please ask for clarification.

units.why: 'The use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is encouraged/required in this course for specific assignments' makes AI use expected in coursework; P79.
units.anchor: is encouraged/required in this course for specific assignments
units.resolution_why: A coded modality should, B informs. The statement tells students that AI 'is encouraged/required in this course for specific assignments': a statement about how the course is built, with the choice between encouraged and required left to the instructor, so informs.

units.why: UMass: learners "must appropriately cite any AI-generated material that informed their work", P24.
units.anchor: learners must appropriately cite any AI-generated material that informed their work
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A permit, B require). The citation duty conditions AI use that the statement encourages, so permit.

units.why: 'Using an AI tool to generate content without proper attribution violates institutional academic integrity policies' makes nondisclosure the violation; P28.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool to generate content without proper attribution violates institutional academic integrity policies.
units.resolution_why: Coders agree on type and codes; unit_stance differs (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence says generating content without attribution violates integrity policy, which limits AI use: restrict.

units.why: The Temple 'welcome/expected' sample says students are 'welcome/expected to use generative AI tools ... as doing so aligns with the course learning goal'; P02 fits, and the link to learning goals is in the note.
units.anchor: You are welcome/expected to use generative AI tools
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work. 'You are welcome/expected to use generative AI tools' states what students may do in their work, so during-work; the link to the course learning goal is a separate unit (P83).
units.fit_note: Justifies use by alignment with a named course learning goal.

units.why: Permission is justified because it "aligns with the course learning goal", tying AI use to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: doing so aligns with the course learning goal
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. The Temple template justifies broad AI use because 'doing so aligns with the course learning goal'; B recorded it only in a fit note. It is a distinct rationale, so kept as P83.

units.why: UMass prohibit template headed "AI is not allowed": "all work is expected to be generated by the learners themselves", a ban on AI for the course's work, so P01 and must-not.
units.anchor: all work is expected to be generated by the learners themselves
units.fit_note: Also says all work is expected to be generated by learners themselves (own-work rule, P29).
units.resolution_why: A coded P29 and modality must; B coded P01 and must-not. The statement is headed 'AI is not allowed:' and says 'all work is expected to be generated by the learners themselves', so the point is a ban on AI for the course's work (P01, must-not); the own-work wording is in the fit note. units.anchor: using artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT

units.anchor: may be considered a violation of UMSL’s Academic Honesty policy and Student Conduct Code

units.anchor: work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B general. 'work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original' applies to work students submit, so during-work.

units.why: "Faculty, students and administrative staff all share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness of the intellectual environment": a fairness and integrity-culture rationale, P95.
units.anchor: share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness of the intellectual environment at UMSL
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. 'Faculty, students and administrative staff all share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness of the intellectual environment at UMSL' is a statement of shared responsibility in the integrity section; B did not code it. Kept as P95.

notes: One included document (UMSL Center for Teaching and Learning sample syllabus statements). Statements from UMass Amherst, Temple and WashU are coded because UMSL offers them to instructors for adoption; they are options, not binding rules. The grade-appeal sentence appears three times and is coded once. Bracketed penalty placeholders are noted in fit_note. Dropped after source check: a purpose-of-guidance clause ('assist you in developing clear and transparent policies'), the purpose clause 'show how AI tools have supported, not replaced, your own thinking' (A: P34, written reflection rather than interview; the rule itself is the P26 reflection unit), the 'Adapted from Perkins et al., 2024' credit line (A: P84, only credits a source), the Temple lead-in sentence 'permitted in this course for the following activities' (A: P05, lists rather than named levels; its items are coded), and A's separate false-quotations unit (folded into the P37 no-credit unit).
